title: When engines play chess
text: For most of the twentieth century, chess engines were useful {{1}} rather than threats: they calculated millions of positions a second but evaluated them like accountants, and grandmasters {{2}} their weaknesses confidently. Then came two quiet {{3}}. Evaluation functions learned to weigh structure, not just material; and in 1997, against Garry Kasparov, a machine crossed the line. The second {{4}} was deeper. Neural networks, trained on millions of games and then on games against themselves, developed a style humans describe as {{5}}: calm, long-term, indifferent to material the way a philosopher is indifferent to pocket change. Today's engines {{6}} the world champion in any format, and human chess has {{7}} around them: opening theory is engine-approved, training is engine-driven, and the style of elite play has visibly {{8}} — sharper, more concrete, quicker to sacrifice. The machines did not end human chess. They raised the ceiling, and the players followed.

gaps.explanation: 'useful tools rather than threats' — instruments of work; toll = a charge or a bell's sound.
'grandmasters exploited their weaknesses' — used them to win; exhort = urge strongly.
'then came two quiet upheavals' — deep disruptions of the established order; upshots are results, and incomes and outputs are quantities.
'the second leap was deeper' — a jump in capability; loom = appear threateningly.
'a style humans describe as serene: calm, long-term' — tranquil; severe = harsh, the opposite of the point.
'engines outplay the world champion' — defeat them in play; outlay = money spent.
'human chess has reorganised around them' — restructured its practice; rebuke = scold.
'the style has visibly matured — sharper, more concrete' — grown up; mellow = soften, which contradicts 'sharper'.
